text: ABSTRACT
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > ABSTRACT

text: Cobalt electrodeposition is the core technology in chip manufacturing. Butynediol (BD) is the key component in cobalt electrodeposition. In this work, the molecule structure and adsorption ability of BD are successfully revealed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The number of transferred electrons (ΔN) value near 0, and the interaction between oxygen atom not alkynyl group in BD and cobalt, demonstrating that BD is physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface. The adsorption energy of BD on hexagonal closepacked (hcp)(101) is −0.67 eV, which is the highest adsorption energy among crystal faces, manifesting that (101) may be a potential preferred orientation. Then the effects of BD on the electroreduction behavior of cobalt is revealed by electro chemical experimental techniques. BD can inhibit the electroreduction of cobalt ions based on kinetics and decreases the diffusion coefficient from 3.43 × 10 − 6 to 1.33 × 10 − 6 cm 2 /s, but the reaction is irreversible with diffusion control whether it contains BD or not. BD can make the charge transfer resistance increase from 241 Ω/cm 2 to 496 Ω/cm 2.
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > ABSTRACT

text: BD has some effects on the cobalt electroreduction kinetics, it does not change the instantaneous nucleation mechanism. Finally, the morphology, composition and structure of the cobalt coating are characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). BD can refine the grains and improving the uniformity of the cobalt coating. Although the properties of the mixed crystals have not changed, the preferred orientation has changed due to the addition of BD. A new peak of hcp(101) arises resulted from the adsorption of BD to form a retained surface, which are consistent with the calculation results. And the relatively positive values of stress change indicates that BD causes the internal stress of cobalt coating to be tensile stress.

text: 1. Introduction
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction

text: Electrodeposition plays a vital role in advanced chip manufacturing as it is a key technology for electrical interconnects. With the rapid development of technology, the length of metal wiring inside the chip has been significantly extended, at the same time, the number of layers inside the chip has also continued to increase. To improve energy efficiency and performance, the size of transistors and metals must continue to shrink [1–4]. However, this process inevitably exacerbates the size effect (grain boundary and interface diffusion of electrons in metals), significantly increases the current load and resistance, and causes serious RC delay and thermal damage to chip performance. Metal cobalt has a small mean free path and low size effect, making it an ideal metal [5].
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction

text: Metal cobalt interconnect layer is mainly prepared by electrodeposition technology. In the process of metal cobalt electrodeposition, additives are key components that can adjust the cobalt deposition rate in via and trench, improve the uniformity of the deposited cobalt film, and thus improve chip performance [6–9]. However, due to the confidentiality of the technology, there are relatively few related studies and reports, but this does not affect its importance and application prospects. Li et al. [10] introduced that dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride could refine cobalt grains and achieve microvia superconformal filling. Huang et al. [11,12] showed that dimethylglyoxime had a strong suppression effect and made cobalt a three-dimensional nucleation. Wu et al. [13] discovered that Akyne-PEG4-amine could be used as an inhibitor to achieve nanometer scale superfilling of cobalt electrode position. Kiruba et al. [14] presented that butynediol (BD) would change the interfacial pH to regulate and control the formation of cobalt. It is worth noting that BD as a typical type-II brightener has attracted much attention among the many cobalt additives. Jeyabharathi et al.
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction

text: [15] deemed that BD would cause electrochemical oscillation due to the hydrogenation of BD during cobalt electrodeposition. Pan et al. [16] showed that BD and saccharin together could decrease the microhard ness of cobalt deposits as a result of increased grain size. Although it is well known that BD can be used as an additive, the effect of its molecular structure on the interface of cobalt electrodeposition has not been elucidated at a molecular level. Therefore, it is necessary to carry out relevant research. This study demonstrates the adsorption state of BD on cobalt surface and the effects of adsorption on crystal growth and orientation. This enriches the understanding of the role of additives in the cobalt electrodeposition process, revealing that BD achieves uniformity and compact film morphology through interactions with the cobalt surface, which is conducive to promote the development of high-performance chip interconnection technology.
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction

text: In this work, the molecule structure, adsorption ability and electrochemical property of BD are revealed through density functional theory (DFT) calculation and electrochemical analyses. The effect of BD on the morphology, composition and structure of the cobalt coating were clarified by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD).

text: 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses

text: Electrochemical analyses were performed using CHI electrochemical workstation (CHI760, China). The basic electrolyte composed of 0.3 MCoSO 4^•7H2 O, 0.16 M H_3BO_3 and 0.02 M CoCl ⋅6 H O. The concentration of additive BD was 0.12 mM. The pH of the electrolyte was adjusted by 5 % H_2 SO_4 aqueous solution and stabilized to 3 ~ 4. The temperature of electrolyte was 303 K. A glassy carbon electrode (GCE) with 3 mm diameter, a H [g/Hg_2SO_4 electrode (saturated K_2SO_4 solution, SMSE) and a platinum sheet were acted as the working electrode, reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. Before experiments, the GCE was firstly polished with 300 nm and 50 nm Al_2O_3 respectively, further ultrasonically cleaned in absolute ethanol and ultrapure water ( 1 8.2 M Ω cm ^- 1). The value of the OCP is about −0.21 V and the stability time is 120 s.

text: 2.3. Electrodeposition and characterization details
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.3. Electrodeposition and characterization details

text: The cobalt electrodeposition experiments were carried out in baths (0.3 M CoSO •7 H O, 0.16 M H_3BO_3 and 0.02 M CoCl _2·6\H_2 O) without and with BD at the temperature of 303 K and the pH of 3–4. The current density was 10 mA/cm2. The electrodeposition time was 10 min. The anode material is cobalt plate (area: 5 × 5 ~ cm ^2, thickness:1 cm), and cathode material is copper sheet (area: 4 × 2 cm ^2,, thickness: 50 μm). The distance between anode and cathode is 6 cm. The morphology of the cobalt coating was characterized by SEM (Zeiss) with an accelerating voltage of 10 kV. Coupled EDS was used to measure the composition. The structure of the cobalt coating was characterized by XRD (Rigaku) with Cu Kα target and wavelength of 0.15406 nm.

text: 2.4. Calculations
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.4. Calculations

text: The DFT calculations of BD molecule were conducted by Gaussian 09 program package [17]. Basis sets of 6–311 + + G ^* \ast ^* for H, C and O atoms was employed with B3LYP functional [18]. The solvent effect of water was included by integral equation formalism polarizable continuum model (IEFPCM). The electrostatic potential (ESP) and average local ionisation energy (ALIE) were calculated by using the Multiwfn package [19–22].
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.4. Calculations

text: The adsorption of BD on cobalt surface at different faces was investigated using the slab model DFT calculations with the generalized Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) [23], and the projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotential plane-wave method on the VASP code [24–28]. A2×2×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid was used for all on geometry optimization calculations. The plane-wave energy cutoff was set to 500 eV. The convergence criterion for the total energy tolerance per atom was 1 × 1 0 ^- 6 eV/atom, and the maximum force tolerance was 0.0 2 : eV ·A^-1

text: 3.1. Number of transferred electrons and frontier molecular orbits
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.1. Number of transferred electrons and frontier molecular orbits

text: The work function of metal and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of molecule can be used to evaluate the electron transfer and the adsorption ability. The work function of cobalt is about 4.70 eV [29], meaning that the Fermi level of cobalt is about −4.70 V (Assumption: the vacuum energy level is 0). The energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (E HOMO) of BDis - 7.5 5 eV. If the Fermi level of the metal is close to the HOMO level of the molecule, the driving force for electrons to transfer from the molecule to the metal surface will decrease. This means that electrons are more likely to transfer between metal and molecule, thereby enhancing the interaction between molecule and metal surface. Obviously, the Fermi level value of cobalt is quite different from the HOMO level value of BD, and the interaction between them is relatively weak. The number of transferred electrons (ΔN) can further analyze the ability of the electron transfer between metal and molecule. when the value of ΔN is close to ^ 0, it means that the electron transfer is not obvious, indicating that the interaction is physical adsorption [30].

text: 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy

text: Adsorption can be divided into physical adsorption and chemical adsorption, which are related to the electrostatic effects and the reactivity of molecule, respectively. To expound the electrostatic effects of BD, the colored isopleth maps of the ESP and the area distribution of ESP spacings on the equivalent surface for BD are displayed in Fig. 2. The red region and blue region represent the higher and lower ESP, respectively. The maximum and minimum values of ESP are expressed by orange and cyan spheres, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2a, it can be seen that the lower ESP is mainly distributed on the oxygen atoms on both sides, and the higher ESP is mainly located in the hydrogen atoms on both sides, indicating that the electrons are mainly concentrated on the oxygen atoms on both sides, and the holes are primarily distributed in the hydrogen atoms on both sides. The highest and lowest ESP values are 52.67 and −43.90 kcal/mol. This uneven distribution of ESP can easily lead to a strong electrostatic effect [33]. Fig. 2b presents the histogram of the area distribution at different ESP intervals for BD.
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy

text: Obviously, BD has a relatively high percentage of area in the low ( 10) regions of ESP. The results again manifest that BD can be adsorbed on metal substances in a strong electrostatic interaction [33], and is mainly physically adsorbed by oxygen atoms.
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy

text: To clarify the reactivity of BD, the ALIE is completed and the results are presented in Fig. 3. The lower the value of ALIE is, the stronger the reactivity is. The cyan spheres represent the lower points of ALIE, which means that these points are easy to attack by electrophilic reaction [33]. The highest and lowest ALIE values are 268.89 and 203.39 kcal/mol. Obviously, the reactive sites are mainly located in the alkynyl group, that is, these regions are prone to chemical adsorption. Moreover, the more spheres there are in the blue regions, the more chemically active the molecule is, and the easier it is to chemically adsorb. Therefore, it can be seen that BD is also prone to chemical adsorption, and the active sites are mainly concentrated at alkynyl group.

text: 3.3. Adsorption on cobalt surface
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.3. Adsorption on cobalt surface

text: Based on the ESP and ALIE results, it can be found that BD may be chemical and physical adsorption, and the adsorption regions are concentrated at the alkynyl group and the oxygen atoms on both sides, respectively. To further understand the adsorption type of BD, the adsorption structure of BD and its adsorption energy on different crystal faces are completed. Cobalt possesses face centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal closepacked (hcp) structures. Fig. 4 presents the adsorption behavior of BD on different fcc and hcp crystal faces. Table 1 and Table 2 show the energy values of the different structures and the corresponding adsorptions, respectively. As shown in Fig. 4, regardless of crystal faces, BD is adsorbed exothermically. At the co-adsorbed structure, there are interactions between oxygen atom in BD and cobalt, verifying that BD is physically adsorbed on the surface of cobalt metal. Furthermore, the adsorption energy of BD on fcc(111), fcc(200), fcc(220), hcp(002), hcp (100) and hcp(101) are −0.34, −0.37, −0.44, −0.38, −0.08 and −0.67 eV, respectively.

text: The results indicate that BD is easily adsorbed on the surface of hcp(101), forming a retention surface, which eventually makes (101) a potential preferred orientation.

It is worth noting that the cathodic peak currents are − 1.9 8 ~ mA/cm2 and − 1.3 0 mA/cm2 without and with BD, indicating that based on kinetics, BD can inhibit the electroreduction of cobalt ions. Moreover, in the more positive potential range ( 0.5 ~ 1.0 V),, the current increases sharply, indicating that metal cobalt is oxidized. The anodic current with BD is less than that without BD, which may be due to the adsorption of BD, hindering the dissolution of cobalt.

text: The chronoamperometric experiments are conducted under different step-potentials to study the cobalt electro-crystallization process. Fig. 9 shows the chronoamperometric curves on GCE in electrolyte without and with BD, respectively. When a certain step potential is applied, a large current is generated in a very short time and then decreases rapidly, which is attributed to the instantaneous charging of the double electric layer. With the extension of time, the current density first increases to a peak value ( j _m, corresponding to the time t _m) _:, and then gradually decreases until it tends to be stable. This is due to the continuous formation and growth of crystal nuclei, and the current density gradually increases, then the number of crystal nuclei continues to increase, the crystal nucleus diffusion area continues to overlap, and the current density reaches a peak value, finally after the diffusion area completely overlaps, there is no nucleation site for new nuclei to generate, only crystal nuclei grow, and the current density gradually decreases until it tends to be stable. If there is no peak current density in the curve, cobalt may grow epitaxially along the substrate.

text: 3.5. Morphology and structure of coating
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.5. Morphology and structure of coating

text: The cobalt electrodeposition at current density of 1 0 mA/cm2 is performed in electrolytes (0.3 M CoSO _4•7H_2 0, 0.16 M H_3BO_3 and 0.02 M CoCl _2·6\H_2 O) without and with BD at the temperature of 303 K and the pH of 3–4. The selection of this current density 1 0 mA/cm2 is based on the actual electrodeposition process and the chronoamperometric curve. First, in the process of cobalt electrodeposition, by selecting 1 0 mA/cm2;, a uniform and dense coating can be obtained. Secondly, according to the chronoamperometric curve, it can be seen that the curve at around 1 0 mA/cm2 is stable, which is consistent with instantaneous nucleation. Instantaneous nucleation can generate a large number of crystal nuclei in a short time, reduce secondary nucleation, reduce the growth size of grains, and make the microstructure of the deposited coating relatively finer. text: 4. Conclusions
section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 4. Conclusions

text: In this work, the molecule structure, adsorption ability and electrochemical property of BD are clarified by using DFT calculation and electrochemical analyses, and the impact on morphology, composition and structure of cobalt coating caused by BD are characterized by SEM combined with EDS and XRD. This work is undoubtedly beneficial to understanding the structural characteristics of BD itself and the effects on electroreduction mechanism of cobalt at a molecular level, and further developing and improving the cobalt electrodeposition process and high-performance chip interconnection technology.
